source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 17 (PDF 4-16, printed 1-13); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 17 (Group 2 Elements), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Group 2 elements are called alkaline earth metals because of:

options.text: their position in the p block
their metallic nature and occurrence in the earth crust

blocks.explanation: They are called alkaline earth metals due to their metallic nature and occurrence in the earth crust (17.1).

book_ref.quote: They are also called the alkaline earth metals due to their metallic nature

blocks.prompt: 2 In reactivity, the Group 2 metals lie between:
blocks.explanation: Group 2 metals have reactivity between highly reactive alkali metals and less reactive transition metals (17.1).

book_ref.quote: having reactivity between highly reactive alkali metals and less reactive transition metals

blocks.prompt: 3 Which two Group 2 elements are among the eight most widely occurring elements in the earth crust?
blocks.explanation: The chapter states that Ca and Mg are among the eight most widely occurring elements in the earth crust (17.1).

book_ref.quote: Ca and Mg are among the eight most widely occurring elements in the earth crust

blocks.prompt: 4 Which Group 2 element is an important part of chlorophyll?
blocks.explanation: Mg is an important part of chlorophyll, the green matter in plants (17.1).

book_ref.quote: Mg is an important part of chlorophyll, the green matter in plants

blocks.prompt: 5 Which Group 2 element is used to make copper alloys harder for aerospace materials?
blocks.explanation: Be is used to make copper alloys harder for aerospace materials (17.1).

book_ref.quote: Be is used to make copper alloys harder for aerospace materials

blocks.prompt: 6 Group 2 elements show similar chemical properties because they all have:

options.text: one electron in the outermost s subshell (ns¹)
two electrons in the outermost s subshell (ns²)
completely filled p subshells as valence shells

blocks.explanation: All Group 2 elements have two electrons in their outermost s subshells (ns²), therefore they exhibit similar chemical properties (17.1).

book_ref.quote: therefore, they exhibit similar chemical properties

blocks.prompt: 7 According to Table 17.1, the electron configuration of strontium is:
blocks.explanation: Strontium (atomic number 38) has the configuration [Kr] 5s² (Table 17.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 17.1 Properties of Group 2 (Be–Ba)

blocks.prompt: 8 From Table 17.1, the metallic radius (pm) changes from Be to Ba as:

options.text: it stays nearly constant at about 160

blocks.explanation: Metallic radius increases down the group: Be 112, Mg 160, Ca 197, Sr 215, Ba 222 pm. The values 31-135 are the M²⁺ ionic radii (Table 17.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 17.1 Properties of Group 2 (Be–Ba)

blocks.prompt: 9 Which Group 2 element has the highest first ionization energy in Table 17.1?
blocks.explanation: First ionization energy falls down the group: Be 900, Mg 738, Ca 590, Sr 550, Ba 503; Be is highest (Table 17.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 17.1 Properties of Group 2 (Be–Ba)

blocks.prompt: 10 Using Table 17.1, the sum of the first and second ionization energies of magnesium is:
blocks.explanation: For Mg: 738 + 1451 = 2189 (table values). 2657 is the sum for Be and 1468 for Ba (Table 17.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 17.1 Properties of Group 2 (Be–Ba)

blocks.prompt: 11 Which Group 2 element has the highest melting point (°C) in Table 17.1?
blocks.explanation: Be has the highest melting point, 1287 °C; the melting points do not fall smoothly (Mg 650 is lower than Ca 842) (Table 17.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 17.1 Properties of Group 2 (Be–Ba)

blocks.prompt: 12 Which Group 2 element has the lowest density in Table 17.1?
blocks.explanation: Densities: Be 1.85, Mg 1.74, Ca 1.54, Sr 2.64, Ba 3.51 g/cm³; Ca is the lowest (Table 17.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 17.1 Properties of Group 2 (Be–Ba)

blocks.prompt: 13 The irregular trends in melting point and density of Group 2 metals are related to:

options.text: the different packing of the metal atoms

blocks.explanation: The trend in melting point and density is related to the different packing of the metal atoms down the group (17.1).

book_ref.quote: The trend in melting point and density are related to the different packing of the metal atoms down the group

blocks.prompt: 14 The standard electrode potential (E°) of Group 2 elements, from Be to Ba:
blocks.explanation: E° becomes more negative from Be to Ba (Ba −2.91 V is the most negative), matching increasing reactivity (Table 17.1).

book_ref.quote: E° becoming more negative from Be to Ba, is unchanged

blocks.prompt: 15 Mg, Ca, Sr and Ba are essential components of fireworks because of their:
blocks.explanation: Mg, Ca, Sr and Ba are essential components of fireworks due to their vibrant flame colours (17.1).

book_ref.quote: Most firework colours are due to Group 2 element

blocks.prompt: 16 Group 2 atoms become stable ions by losing two electrons. The ion formed is:
blocks.explanation: After losing the two ns² electrons they become stable ions with a +2 charge, M²⁺ (17.1.1).

book_ref.quote: After losing these two electrons, they become stable ions with a +2 charge (M²⁺)

blocks.prompt: 17 Which statement correctly explains why reactivity increases from Be to Ba?

options.text: Size and shielding increase while ionization energy decreases
Size decreases and ionization energy increases
Nuclear charge felt by valence electrons increases
The number of valence electrons increases

blocks.explanation: Down the group size and shielding increase and ionization energy decreases, so removal of electrons is easier and reactivity increases (17.1.1).

book_ref.quote: The reactivity increases from Be to Ba due to the increase in size, shielding effect and decrease in the ionization energy down the group

blocks.prompt: 18 The correct reactivity order of Group 2 elements is:
blocks.explanation: The reactivity series increases from Be to Ba: Be < Mg < Ca < Sr < Ba; Be is least and Ba most reactive (17.1.1).

book_ref.quote: It shows that Be is the least reactive and Ba is the most reactive element of Group 2

blocks.prompt: 19 Down Group 2, the removal of the valence electrons becomes:
blocks.explanation: Larger size, more shielding and lower ionization energy make the removal of electrons easier down the group (17.1.1).

book_ref.quote: This makes the removal of electrons easier, and the reactivity increases

blocks.prompt: 20 When a Group 2 metal M burns in oxygen, the general product is:
blocks.explanation: All Group 2 metals burn in oxygen to form metal oxides MO: 2M + O₂ → 2MO (17.2.1).

book_ref.quote: All Group 2 metals burn in oxygen to form metal oxides (MO)

blocks.prompt: 21 Beryllium is less reactive towards oxygen than the other Group 2 members because:

options.text: a thin, strong oxide layer protects it

blocks.explanation: Be reacts with oxygen only at high temperatures (above 600 °C); a thin, strong oxide layer usually protects it (17.2.1).

book_ref.quote: A thin, strong oxide layer usually protects it

blocks.prompt: 22 Beryllium reacts with oxygen to form BeO at temperatures:
blocks.explanation: Beryllium reacts with oxygen at high temperatures (above 600 °C) to form BeO (17.2.1).

book_ref.quote: reacts with oxygen at high temperatures

blocks.prompt: 23 Calcium burns in oxygen with a:
blocks.explanation: The reaction of Ca with oxygen is more vigorous and gives a brick red flame (17.2.1).

book_ref.quote: The reaction of calcium (Ca) with oxygen is more vigorous to give a brick red flame

blocks.prompt: 24 Magnesium burns brightly in air to form:
blocks.explanation: Mg burns brightly in air or oxygen to form magnesium oxide, MgO (17.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Magnesium (Mg) burns brightly in air or oxygen to form magnesium oxide (MgO)

blocks.prompt: 25 The oxides of Group 2 elements are generally:

options.text: white solids, basic, more basic down the group
white solids, acidic, more acidic down the group

blocks.explanation: Group 2 oxides are generally white solids, basic in nature, and their basic character increases down the group (17.2.1).

book_ref.quote: generally white solids and basic in nature and their basic character increases down the group

blocks.prompt: 26 When one oxide ion of a Group 2 oxide reacts with water, the number of hydroxide ions produced is:
blocks.explanation: The oxide ion reacts with water to produce hydroxide ions: O²⁻(s) + H₂O(l) → 2OH⁻(aq) (17.2.1).

book_ref.quote: due to the reaction between the oxide ion and water to produce the OH⁻ ion

blocks.prompt: 27 Which statement about beryllium and water is correct?

options.text: Be reacts explosively with cold water
Be reacts with steam to give BeO and H₂
Be does not react with water or steam even when heated
Be reacts slowly with cold water to give Be(OH)₂

blocks.explanation: Beryllium does not react with water or steam, even when heated, due to its protective oxide layer (17.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Beryllium (Be) does not react with water or steam, even when heated

blocks.prompt: 28 Group 2 metals (except Be) react with water to give:
blocks.explanation: Except Be, Group 2 metals react with water to produce metal hydroxides M(OH)₂ and hydrogen gas (17.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Except beryllium (Be), other Group 2 metals react with water to produce metal hydroxides

blocks.prompt: 29 The magnesium compound formed with steam differs from that formed with cold water. With steam the product is:
blocks.explanation: With steam Mg reacts faster: Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g) (17.2.2).

book_ref.quote: With steam, it reacts faster to form magnesium oxide (MgO) and hydrogen

blocks.prompt: 30 The reaction of magnesium with cold water is:

options.text: very slow, giving Mg(OH)₂ and H₂

blocks.explanation: Mg reacts very slowly with cold water forming Mg(OH)₂ and H₂; with steam it reacts faster (17.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Magnesium (Mg) reacts very slowly with cold water, forming Mg(OH)₂ and H₂

blocks.prompt: 31 When calcium reacts with water, a white precipitate appears because:

options.text: Ca does not react at all

blocks.explanation: Ca reacts with cold water vigorously to give Ca(OH)₂ and H₂; Ca(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble and forms a white precipitate (17.2.2).

book_ref.quote: The calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble, forming a white precipitate

blocks.prompt: 32 Compared with magnesium, calcium reacts with cold water:
blocks.explanation: Calcium reacts with cold water and steam more vigorously than magnesium (17.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Calcium (Ca) reacts with cold water and steam more vigorously than magnesium

blocks.prompt: 33 The basic character of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group due to:
blocks.explanation: Group 2 hydroxides are less basic than those of Group 1, but their basic character increases down the group due to increasing solubility (17.2.2).

book_ref.quote: The hydroxides of Group 2 are less basic than the Group 1 elements

blocks.prompt: 34 Group 2 metals react with dilute hydrochloric acid to form:
blocks.explanation: M(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MCl₂(aq) + H₂(g): a salt and hydrogen gas (17.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Group 2 metals react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas

blocks.prompt: 35 The reaction of beryllium with dilute acids can be slow because of:
blocks.explanation: Be reacts with dilute acids to form BeCl₂ and H₂, but its protective oxide layer can slow the reaction (17.2.3).

book_ref.quote: but its protective oxide layer can slow this reaction

blocks.prompt: 36 The reaction of calcium with dilute sulphuric acid can stop early because:

options.text: calcium does not react with acids
sparingly soluble CaSO₄ coats the metal surface
CaSO₄ is a gas that escapes

blocks.explanation: CaSO₄ formed is sparingly soluble and coats the metal surface with a protective layer, stopping the reaction early (17.2.3).

book_ref.quote: the reaction can stop early because the calcium sulphate (CaSO₄) formed is sparingly soluble

blocks.prompt: 37 Magnesium reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to give:
blocks.explanation: Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g) (17.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Magnesium (Mg) reacts readily with dilute acids

blocks.prompt: 38 Which equation for calcium with dilute HCl is correctly balanced?
blocks.explanation: Ca(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂(g); Ca forms Ca²⁺, so two Cl⁻ are needed (17.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Calcium (Ca) reacts vigorously with dilute acids to form calcium salts and hydrogen gas

blocks.prompt: 39 If 0.5 mol of a Group 2 metal reacts completely with excess dilute HCl, the amount of H₂ formed is:
blocks.explanation: M + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂: 1 mol M gives 1 mol H₂, so 0.5 mol M gives 0.5 mol H₂ (17.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Group 2 metals react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas

blocks.prompt: 40 The key differences between Group 1 and Group 2 metals are mainly due to differences in their:
blocks.explanation: Group 1 and Group 2 show key differences due to the difference in their ionization energies (17.3).

book_ref.quote: they show key differences due to the difference in their ionization energies

blocks.prompt: 41 Group 2 metals are generally less reactive than Group 1 metals of the same period because:

options.text: losing two electrons requires more energy
they have only one valence electron

blocks.explanation: Group 2 metals lose two electrons, which requires more energy, so they are less reactive than Group 1 metals in the same period (17.3).

book_ref.quote: Group 2 metals lose two electrons, which requires more energy

blocks.prompt: 42 Which property belongs to Group 1 metals rather than Group 2 metals?

options.text: Very soft, can be cut with a knife

blocks.explanation: Group 1 metals are very soft (can be cut with a knife); Group 2 metals are harder, form M²⁺ and MO, and have higher melting points (Table 17.2).

book_ref.quote: Very soft (can be cut with a knife).

blocks.prompt: 43 The oxides of Group 1 and Group 2 metals have the general formulae respectively:
blocks.explanation: Group 1 forms M₂O (e.g., Na₂O), highly basic; Group 2 forms MO (e.g., CaO), less basic (Table 17.2).

book_ref.quote: Form M₂O (e.g., Na₂O); highly basic.

blocks.prompt: 44 Which example in Table 17.2 shows the less vigorous reaction of Group 2 metals with water?

options.text: Ca with water, Mg with steam

blocks.explanation: Group 1 reacts very vigorously, often explosively (Na with water); Group 2 less vigorously (Ca with water, Mg with steam) (Table 17.2).

book_ref.quote: Less vigorous (e.g., Ca with water, Mg with steam).

blocks.prompt: 45 Compared with Group 1 metals, Group 2 metals have:

options.text: higher densities and higher melting points
lower densities and lower melting points
lower densities and higher melting points

blocks.explanation: Group 2 metals have higher densities and higher melting/boiling points than Group 1 metals (Table 17.2).

book_ref.quote: Higher densities than Group 1 metals.

blocks.prompt: 46 Compared with Group 1 hydroxides, Group 2 hydroxides are:
blocks.explanation: Group 2 hydroxides are less soluble than Group 1 (solubility increases down the group) and less basic than Group 1 hydroxides (Table 17.2).

book_ref.quote: Less soluble than Group 1, but solubility increases down the group

blocks.prompt: 47 In both Group 1 and Group 2, reactivity going down the group:
blocks.explanation: Both groups show increasing reactivity down the group due to increasing atomic size and decreasing ionization energy (17.3).

book_ref.quote: Both groups show increasing reactivity going down their respective groups

blocks.text: 17.4 Thermal Decomposition of Carbonates and Nitrates

blocks.prompt: 48 A reaction in which a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances on heating is called:
blocks.explanation: Thermal decomposition is a chemical reaction where a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances when heated (17.4).

book_ref.quote: Thermal decomposition is a chemical reaction, where a single compound breaks down

blocks.prompt: 49 Thermal decomposition is usually:
blocks.explanation: It usually requires energy (endothermic) to break the chemical bonds within the compound (17.4).

book_ref.quote: This process usually requires energy (endothermic)

blocks.prompt: 50 On heating, MgCO₃ decomposes to give:
blocks.explanation: Group 2 carbonates decompose to MO and CO₂: MgCO₃(s) → MgO(s) + CO₂(g) (17.4).

book_ref.quote: Group 2 carbonates decompose upon heating to form a metal oxide (MO) and carbon dioxide gas

blocks.prompt: 51 The correct order of increasing thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates is:
blocks.explanation: Thermal stability of carbonates increases down the group; BaCO₃ requires the highest temperature (1360 °C) to decompose (17.4).

book_ref.quote: BaCO₃ requires the highest temperature to decompose

blocks.prompt: 52 According to Table 17.3, which carbonate decomposes at 900 °C?
blocks.explanation: Table 17.3: BeCO₃ 250, MgCO₃ 540, CaCO₃ 900, SrCO₃ 1289, BaCO₃ 1360 °C (17.4).

book_ref.quote: Table 17.3 Temperatures of decomposition of the Group 2 carbonates at 1 atm

blocks.prompt: 53 From Table 17.3, how much higher is the decomposition temperature of CaCO₃ than that of MgCO₃?

book_ref.quote: Table 17.3 Temperatures of decomposition of the Group 2 carbonates at 1 atm

blocks.prompt: 54 BeCO₃ decomposes at a lower temperature than BaCO₃ because Be²⁺:

options.text: is large and has low polarizing power
is small and has greater polarizing power

blocks.explanation: Small, highly charged Be²⁺ has greater polarizing power; it distorts the large CO₃²⁻ ion more, weakening its bonds (17.4).

book_ref.quote: Smaller and highly charged cations (like Be²⁺) have a greater

blocks.prompt: 55 Down Group 2, the polarizing power of M²⁺ and the thermal stability of the carbonates respectively:
blocks.explanation: As M²⁺ gets larger its polarizing power decreases, so carbonates become more stable and need more heat to decompose (17.4).

book_ref.quote: As the metal ion gets larger down the group, its polarizing power decreases

blocks.prompt: 56 Which substance is NOT a product of the thermal decomposition of a Group 2 nitrate?
blocks.explanation: Group 2 nitrates decompose to metal oxide, brown NO₂ gas and O₂ (17.4).

book_ref.quote: brown nitrogen dioxide gas (NO₂), and oxygen gas (O₂)

blocks.prompt: 57 The colour of the gas NO₂ given off when Group 2 nitrates are heated is:
blocks.explanation: Heating Group 2 nitrates gives brown nitrogen dioxide gas, NO₂ (17.4).

book_ref.quote: brown nitrogen dioxide gas (NO₂), and oxygen gas (O₂)

blocks.prompt: 58 Which Group 2 nitrate is the least thermally stable?
blocks.explanation: The thermal stability of nitrates increases down Group 2; Be(NO₃)₂ is the least stable and Ba(NO₃)₂ the most stable (17.4).

book_ref.quote: Be(NO₃)₂ is the least stable, and Ba(NO₃)₂ is the most stable among them

blocks.prompt: 59 Nitrates at the top of Group 2 decompose at lower temperatures because the small M²⁺ ions:

options.text: distort the nitrate ion more effectively

blocks.explanation: The smaller M²⁺ ions at the top distort the NO₃⁻ ion more effectively, making its decomposition easier (17.4).

book_ref.quote: distort the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) more effectively

blocks.prompt: 60 In the balanced equation 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + x NO₂ + O₂, the value of x is:
blocks.explanation: 2Ca(NO₃)₂ has 4 N atoms, so 4NO₂ is formed: 2Ca(NO₃)₂(s) → 2CaO(s) + 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g) (17.4).

book_ref.quote: brown nitrogen dioxide gas (NO₂), and oxygen gas (O₂)

blocks.prompt: 61 Observing the temperature at which a Group 2 carbonate decomposes helps chemists to:
blocks.explanation: By observing the decomposition temperature, chemists can identify unknown compounds and confirm specific elements (17.4).

book_ref.quote: chemists can identify the unknown compounds and confirm the presence of specific elements

blocks.prompt: 62 The energy released when gaseous ions are surrounded and attracted by water molecules is the:
blocks.explanation: Enthalpy of hydration (ΔHhyd) is the energy released when gaseous ions are hydrated; it is always exothermic (17.5).

book_ref.quote: is the energy released when gaseous ions are surrounded and attracted by water molecules

blocks.prompt: 63 The signs of ΔHhyd and ΔHlattice (as defined in the chapter) are respectively:
blocks.explanation: ΔHhyd is always exothermic (negative); lattice enthalpy, the energy required to break the solid into gaseous ions, is always endothermic (17.5).

book_ref.quote: This is always exothermic (negative value)

blocks.prompt: 64 Which Group 2 ion has the most negative enthalpy of hydration?
blocks.explanation: Smaller ions with higher charge density attract water more strongly; ΔHhyd becomes less negative down the group, so Be²⁺ is most negative (17.5).

book_ref.quote: Smaller ions with higher charge density attract water molecules more strongly

blocks.prompt: 65 Lattice enthalpy, as defined in the chapter, is the energy:

options.text: needed to remove one electron from an atom
required to break one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions

blocks.explanation: Lattice enthalpy is the energy required to break apart one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions; it is always endothermic (17.5).

book_ref.quote: is the energy required to break apart one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions

blocks.prompt: 66 Lattice energy is higher when:

options.text: one ion is much larger than the other
the sizes of the cation and anion are comparable

blocks.explanation: When the cation and anion sizes are comparable the forces are stronger and lattice energy is higher; a large-small pair gives weaker forces (17.5).

book_ref.quote: As the sizes of the cation and the anion are comparable, the attractive forces become stronger

blocks.prompt: 67 Higher solubility is generally favoured by an enthalpy of solution (ΔHsoln) that is:
blocks.explanation: ΔHsoln is the overall energy change on dissolving; a more negative or less positive value generally favours higher solubility (17.5).

book_ref.quote: A more negative or less positive ΔHsoln generally favours higher solubility

blocks.prompt: 68 Which Group 2 hydroxide is the most soluble in water?
blocks.explanation: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group; Ba(OH)₂ is quite soluble, Mg(OH)₂ sparingly soluble (17.5).

book_ref.quote: The solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group

blocks.prompt: 69 The solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group because, going down:

options.text: hydration enthalpy decreases more than lattice enthalpy
lattice enthalpy decreases more than hydration enthalpy

blocks.explanation: Both ΔHhyd and ΔHlattice decrease down the group, but for hydroxides the decrease in lattice enthalpy is more significant (17.5).

book_ref.quote: the decrease in lattice enthalpy is more significant than the decrease in hydration enthalpy

blocks.prompt: 70 The correct order of decreasing solubility of Group 2 sulphates in water is:
blocks.explanation: Solubility of Group 2 sulphates decreases down the group: MgSO₄ is soluble, BaSO₄ insoluble (17.5).

book_ref.quote: in water decreases down the group (e.g., MgSO₄ is soluble and BaSO₄ is insoluble)

blocks.prompt: 71 The solubility of Group 2 sulphates decreases down the group because, for the large sulphate ion:

options.text: lattice enthalpy decreases more than hydration enthalpy
hydration enthalpy decreases more than lattice enthalpy

blocks.explanation: The SO₄²⁻ ion is relatively large, so the lattice enthalpy changes little; the decrease in hydration enthalpy is more significant (17.5).

book_ref.quote: for a large anion like sulphate, the decrease in hydration enthalpy is more significant

blocks.prompt: 72 Using Table 17.4, how many times more soluble (in mol/100 g of water) is Ba(OH)₂ than Mg(OH)₂?

book_ref.quote: Table 17.4 Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides and sulphates

blocks.prompt: 73 According to Table 17.4, the solubility of BaSO₄ at 298 K is:
blocks.explanation: BaSO₄ 9.43 × 10⁻⁷ mol/100 g; MgSO₄ 1.83 × 10⁻¹, CaSO₄ 4.66 × 10⁻³, Ba(OH)₂ 1.5 × 10⁻² (Table 17.4).

book_ref.quote: Table 17.4 Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides and sulphates

blocks.prompt: 74 Which pair shows opposite solubility trends down Group 2?
blocks.explanation: Hydroxide solubility rises from Mg(OH)₂ to Ba(OH)₂ while sulphate solubility falls from MgSO₄ to BaSO₄ (Table 17.4, Figure 17.4).

book_ref.quote: Table 17.4 Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides and sulphates

blocks.prompt: 75 Because the sulphate ion is large, the lattice enthalpy of Group 2 sulphates down the group:

options.text: changes more than the hydration enthalpy does
changes less than the hydration enthalpy does

blocks.explanation: SO₄²⁻ is relatively large; both enthalpies decrease down the group, but the decrease in hydration enthalpy is more significant than that in lattice enthalpy (17.5).

book_ref.quote: The sulphate ion (SO₄²⁻) is relatively larger

blocks.prompt: 76 Among the Group 2 hydroxides, the highest lattice energy is shown by the one with:
blocks.explanation: With smaller Group 2 metal ions the lattice energy of hydroxides is higher, and vice versa (17.5).

book_ref.quote: With smaller Group 2 metal ions, the lattice energy of hydroxides is higher

blocks.prompt: 77 An ion in which a central metal is bonded to a number of surrounding electron donating species is a:
blocks.explanation: This is the chapter's definition of a complex ion (17.6).

book_ref.quote: A complex ion is an ion in which a central metal is bonded to a number of surrounding electron donating species

blocks.prompt: 78 In a complex ion the central metal ion acts as a:
blocks.explanation: The central metal ion is a Lewis acid (electron pair acceptor); H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, OH⁻ are Lewis bases (17.6).

book_ref.quote: The central metal ion acts as a Lewis acid (electron pair acceptor)

blocks.prompt: 79 The number of coordinate bonds formed between the central metal ion and the electron donors is called the:
blocks.explanation: The number of coordinate bonds between the central ion and the donors is the coordination number; common values are 2, 4 and 6 (17.6).

book_ref.quote: is called coordination number

blocks.prompt: 80 Common coordination numbers mentioned in the chapter are:
blocks.explanation: Common coordination numbers are 2, 4, and 6 (17.6).

book_ref.quote: Common coordination numbers are 2, 4, and 6

blocks.prompt: 81 Complex ion formation is more typical for transition metals because they have:
blocks.explanation: Complex formation is more typical for transition metals due to their available d-orbitals for bonding (17.6).

book_ref.quote: more typical for transition metals (due to their available d-orbitals for bonding)

blocks.prompt: 82 Smaller Group 2 ions are better at attracting electron-donating species because they have:

options.text: a lower charge to size ratio
a higher charge to size ratio

blocks.explanation: The ability to form complexes depends on size and charge; smaller ions have higher charge density and attract donors better (17.6).

book_ref.quote: Smaller ions have a higher charge density (high charge to size ratio)

blocks.prompt: 83 The hydrated beryllium ion has the formula:
blocks.explanation: Be²⁺, the smallest Group 2 ion, forms [Be(H₂O)₄]²⁺ with coordination number 4 (17.6).

book_ref.quote: forms a hydrated ion with a coordination number of 4

blocks.prompt: 84 The coordination number of magnesium in its usual hydrated ion [Mg(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is:
blocks.explanation: Mg²⁺ ions are larger and usually form hexahydrate complexes with coordination number 6 (17.6).

book_ref.quote: Magnesium ions are larger and usually form hexahydrate complexes

blocks.prompt: 85 For the hydrated ions of Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺ and Ba²⁺, the strength of the ion-water interaction down the group:
blocks.explanation: Larger ions form hydrated ions mostly with coordination number 6, though the strength of interaction decreases down the group (17.6).

book_ref.quote: though the strength of the interaction decreases down the group

blocks.prompt: 86 EDTA, which forms a ring complex with Ca²⁺, is a donor of how many electron pairs?
blocks.explanation: Ca²⁺ forms a complex ring structure with EDTA, a six electron pair donor: Ca²⁺ + EDTA⁴⁻ → [Ca(EDTA)]²⁻ (17.6).

book_ref.quote: Calcium ion forms a complex ring structure with a six electron pair donor, EDTA

blocks.prompt: 87 The charge on the complex formed in Ca²⁺ + EDTA⁴⁻ → [Ca(EDTA)] is:
blocks.explanation: (+2) + (−4) = −2, so the complex is [Ca(EDTA)]²⁻ (17.6).

book_ref.quote: Calcium ion forms a complex ring structure with a six electron pair donor, EDTA

blocks.prompt: 88 EDTA complex formation with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ is used in:
blocks.explanation: EDTA removes Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions from hard water (water softening), and can remove toxic metal ions from the body (17.6).

book_ref.quote: This complex formation is used in water softening

blocks.prompt: 89 Donors that form more than one coordinate bond to the same metal ion create:
blocks.explanation: Donors with more than one donatable electron pair can form more than one coordinate bond to the same metal ion, creating a ring-like structure (17.6).

book_ref.quote: can form stable complexes with the donors having more than one donatable electron pairs

blocks.prompt: 90 The Dow process is used to extract:
blocks.explanation: The Dow process is a multi-step chemical and electrochemical process to extract Mg metal from Mg²⁺ ions in seawater (17.7.1).

book_ref.quote: used to extract magnesium metal from the vast reserves of magnesium ions

blocks.prompt: 91 In the Dow process, magnesium ions in seawater are first precipitated by adding:
blocks.explanation: Seawater is treated with Ca(OH)₂: Mg²⁺(aq) + Ca(OH)₂(s) → Mg(OH)₂(s) + Ca²⁺(aq) (17.7.1).

book_ref.quote: which precipitates magnesium as insoluble magnesium hydroxide

blocks.prompt: 92 In the Dow process, Mg(OH)₂ is converted into MgCl₂ by reaction with:
blocks.explanation: Mg(OH)₂(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l) (17.7.1).

book_ref.quote: Magnesium hydroxide is filtered and then reacted with hydrochloric acid (HCl)

blocks.prompt: 93 In the electrolysis of molten MgCl₂, the products at the cathode and anode respectively are:
blocks.explanation: Electrolysis of molten MgCl₂ produces pure Mg at the cathode and Cl₂ gas at the anode (17.7.1).

book_ref.quote: produces pure magnesium metal at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode

blocks.prompt: 94 The final step of the Dow process that produces magnesium metal is:
blocks.explanation: The MgCl₂ solution is concentrated and dried, and molten MgCl₂ is electrolysed in large electrolytic cells (17.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The molten MgCl₂ is subjected to electrolysis in large electrolytic cells

blocks.prompt: 95 In the electrolysis of molten MgCl₂ (Mg = 24, Cl = 35.5 g mol⁻¹), the mass of magnesium obtained from 190 g of MgCl₂ is:
blocks.explanation: M(MgCl₂) = 24 + 71 = 95 g mol⁻¹; 190/95 = 2 mol MgCl₂ gives 2 mol Mg = 2 × 24 = 48 g (Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ → Mg + Cl₂) (17.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The molten MgCl₂ is subjected to electrolysis in large electrolytic cells

blocks.prompt: 96 The Dow process is famous because it extracts magnesium from:
blocks.explanation: It is famous for extracting a valuable metal from an abundant, low-concentration source (seawater) on a massive industrial scale (17.7.1).

book_ref.quote: from an abundant, low-concentration source (sea water) on a massive industrial scale

blocks.prompt: 97 Quicklime is produced by heating limestone in a lime kiln at a typical temperature of:
blocks.explanation: Limestone is heated in a lime kiln to typically 900-1000 °C (calcination); the printed kiln labels are corrected to this range (17.7.2).

book_ref.quote: in a process called calcination or thermal decomposition

blocks.prompt: 98 Limestone is composed primarily of:
blocks.explanation: Limestone is a naturally abundant sedimentary rock composed primarily of CaCO₃ (17.7.2).

book_ref.quote: Limestone is a naturally abundant sedimentary rock composed primarily of calcium carbonate

blocks.prompt: 99 In a lime kiln, CO₂ is removed continuously so that:

options.text: the equilibrium shifts to the right, giving more CaO

blocks.explanation: CaCO₃ ⇌ CaO + CO₂ is reversible in a closed container; removing CO₂ shifts the equilibrium to the right and gives more product faster (17.7.2).

book_ref.quote: This removal shifts the equilibrium to the right

blocks.prompt: 100 The chemical name of quicklime is:
blocks.explanation: Quicklime, or calcium oxide (CaO), is made by heating limestone: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (17.7.2).

book_ref.quote: The production of quicklime involves heating limestone in a high-temperature furnace

blocks.prompt: 101 Heating 50 g of pure CaCO₃ completely (CaCO₃ = 100 g mol⁻¹, CaO = 56 g mol⁻¹) gives a mass of CaO of:
blocks.explanation: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂: 50/100 = 0.5 mol CaCO₃ gives 0.5 mol CaO = 0.5 × 56 = 28 g (17.7.2).

book_ref.quote: The production of quicklime involves heating limestone in a high-temperature furnace

blocks.prompt: 102 In modern lime kilns the ingredients are heated by:

options.text: circulating hot gases at the reaction temperature

blocks.explanation: In modern lime kilns the ingredients are heated by circulating hot gases at the reaction temperature (17.7.2).

book_ref.quote: In modern lime kilns, the ingredients are heated by circulating hot gases

blocks.text: 17.8 Uses of Group 2 Elements and Compounds

blocks.prompt: 103 The diverse uses of Group 2 compounds are largely due to their:
blocks.explanation: Group 2 compounds have diverse uses largely due to their basic nature and varying solubility (17.8).

book_ref.quote: largely due to their basic nature and varying solubility

blocks.prompt: 104 Gypsum, used to make plasterboard and plaster of Paris, is:
blocks.explanation: Calcium sulphate CaSO₄·2H₂O (gypsum) makes plasterboard (drywall) and plaster of Paris, CaSO₄·½H₂O (17.8.1).

book_ref.quote: is used to make plasterboard (drywall)

blocks.prompt: 105 Calcium carbonate is found naturally as:
blocks.explanation: CaCO₃ is found as limestone, marble and chalk, used in building, cement, concrete, and as a filler in paper and plastics (17.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) is found as limestone, marble, and chalk

blocks.prompt: 106 Slaked lime is the common name of:
blocks.explanation: Calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, is slaked lime; CaO is quicklime. Both are used in cement, mortar and plaster (17.8.1).

book_ref.quote: is used in making cement, mortar, and plaster

blocks.prompt: 107 In flue gas desulphurization, CaO and CaCO₃ are used to remove:
blocks.explanation: CaO and CaCO₃ are used in flue gas desulphurization (wet scrubbing) to remove acidic SO₂ from power plant emissions, preventing acid rain (17.8.1).

book_ref.quote: to remove acidic sulphur dioxide (SO₂) from power plant emission

blocks.prompt: 108 Which Group 2 compound is used to line furnaces because of its high melting point?
blocks.explanation: Magnesium oxide is used as a refractory material (lining furnaces) due to its high melting point (17.8.1).

book_ref.quote: is used as a refractory material (lining furnaces) due to its high melting point

blocks.prompt: 109 Red colour in fireworks and flares is produced by compounds of:
blocks.explanation: Strontium compounds are used to produce red colour in fireworks and flares (17.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Strontium compounds are used to produce red colour in fireworks and flares

blocks.prompt: 110 Beryllium is used in X-ray tubes because it is:
blocks.explanation: Beryllium is used in X-ray tubes as it is transparent to X-rays; it also strengthens alloys (17.8.1).

book_ref.quote: in X-ray tubes as it is transparent to X-rays

blocks.prompt: 111 In steel production, quicklime is used to:
blocks.explanation: Quicklime is also used in steel production to remove impurities (17.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Quicklime is also used in the steel production to remove impurities

blocks.prompt: 112 Milk of Magnesia, used to neutralize excess stomach acid, is:
blocks.explanation: Mg(OH)₂ (Milk of Magnesia) neutralizes excess stomach acid and is a mild laxative; its low solubility makes it safe (17.8.2).

book_ref.quote: is used to neutralize excess stomach acid and as a mild laxative

blocks.prompt: 113 Barium meals used for X-ray imaging of the digestive system contain:
blocks.explanation: BaSO₄ is opaque to X-rays and safe because it is highly insoluble and passes through the body without being absorbed (17.8.2).

book_ref.quote: for X-ray imaging of the digestive system

blocks.prompt: 114 Barium sulphate is safe to swallow for X-ray imaging because it is:
blocks.explanation: BaSO₄ is safe because it is highly insoluble and passes through the body without being absorbed (17.8.2).

book_ref.quote: It is opaque to X-rays and is safe because

blocks.prompt: 115 The formula of Epsom salt is:
blocks.explanation: Epsom salts are MgSO₄·7H₂O, used as a laxative and in baths (17.8.2).

book_ref.quote: Epsom salts (MgSO₄·7H₂O) are used as a laxative and in baths

blocks.prompt: 116 Which calcium compound is used in indigestion tablets as an antacid?
blocks.explanation: Calcium carbonate is also used in indigestion tablets as an antacid (17.8.2).

book_ref.quote: is also used in indigestion tablets as an antacid

blocks.prompt: 117 Calcium compounds such as calcium carbonate and calcium citrate are taken as dietary supplements to prevent:
blocks.explanation: Calcium compounds are essential for strong bones and teeth and are used as supplements to prevent osteoporosis (17.8.2).

book_ref.quote: widely used as dietary calcium supplements to prevent osteoporosis

blocks.prompt: 118 CaCO₃ and Ca(OH)₂ are added to acidic soils in order to:
blocks.explanation: They are added to acidic soils to increase pH (neutralize acidity), making soil more suitable for crops (17.8.3).

book_ref.quote: are added to acidic soils to increase pH (neutralize acidity)

blocks.prompt: 119 In plants, calcium and magnesium are needed respectively for:
blocks.explanation: Calcium is crucial for cell wall development, while magnesium is a central atom in chlorophyll (17.8.3).

book_ref.quote: magnesium is a central atom in chlorophyll

blocks.prompt: 120 Which Group 2 compound named in the chapter can be used as a fertilizer?
blocks.explanation: Compounds like calcium nitrate or magnesium sulphate (Epsom salts) can be used as fertilizers (17.8.3).

book_ref.quote: Compounds like calcium nitrate or magnesium sulphate (Epsom salts) can be used as fertilizers
